summary: Describes an RTP payload format for H.264 video, excluding the scalable and multiview extensions, which allows packetizing NAL units for network transport. It obsoletes RFC 3984 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: H.264 is a way to squeeze video. This says how to chop up squeezed video into packets for the internet.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for h.264
what is fu-a fragmentation in rtp
subtitle: How to carry H.264 video in RTP packets: single NAL units, aggregation packets, fragments, and optional reordering.

tldr.problem: H.264 encoders produce NAL units of very different sizes, while networks have different packet size limits and may lose or reorder packets, so the video needs a defined way to ride in RTP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three payload structures (single NAL unit packets, aggregation packets that bundle several NAL units, and fragmentation units that split one NAL unit), three packetization modes, a decoding order number for reordering, and media type parameters for SDP.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3984 and is a Proposed Standard. It adds new media type parameters and clarifies the SDP Offer/Answer rules, with some compatibility caveats for parameter sets sent out of band.

facts.label: NAL unit header
facts.value: 1 byte: F (1 bit), NRI (2 bits), Type (5 bits)

today: RFC 6184 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3984, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself excludes the scalable and multiview extensions, whose payload formats are defined elsewhere.

sections.title: H.264, NAL Units and Parameter Sets
sections.content:
This RFC specifies an RTP payload format for ITU-T Recommendation H.264, also known as Advanced Video Coding (AVC). The codec splits into a Video Coding Layer, which does the signal processing and outputs slices, and a Network Abstraction Layer (NAL), which wraps slices into NAL units suited to packet networks. A NAL unit is a one-byte header plus a payload, and this payload format is unaware of what is inside the payload bytes.

Decoding depends on parameter sets (sequence and picture parameter sets) that hold information such as picture size. They should be sent reliably and in advance of the slices that use them, although they can also be sent in-band. The scope is the "naked" NAL unit stream, not the Annex B bytestream format. The scalable (SVC) and multiview (MVC) extensions are excluded.

H.264 separates transmission, decoding and presentation time. Some NAL units, such as parameter sets and SEI messages, have no timing of their own, so they take the RTP timestamp of the picture they belong to.
sections.eli5: A video is chopped into small labelled pieces. A few special pieces hold the instructions for reading all the others, so they need to arrive safely and first.

sections.title: RTP Header and NAL Unit Header
sections.content:
The payload uses the RTP header of RFC 3550 consistently. The marker bit is set on the very last packet of an access unit, and for an aggregation packet it takes the value the last NAL unit would have had alone. A 90 kHz clock rate MUST be used for the timestamp. The payload type is assigned dynamically or by profile, outside this document.

The first byte of every payload is a NAL unit header: F (1 bit), NRI (2 bits) and Type (5 bits). F set to 1 means the unit may contain bit errors or syntax violations, and MANEs SHOULD set it when they detect errors. NRI of 00 means the content is not used for reference pictures and can be discarded safely. Non-zero NRI values also show relative transport priority, with 11 the highest. Encoders SHOULD set NRI to 11 for sequence and picture parameter sets and for IDR slices.
sections.eli5: Every envelope starts with a small label that says what is inside, whether it might be damaged, and how important it is.

sections.title: Single, Aggregated and Fragmented Packets
sections.content:
The first byte of the payload tells the receiver which of three structures follows. Types 1 to 23 are a single NAL unit packet that carries exactly one NAL unit. Types 24 to 27 are aggregation packets (STAP-A, STAP-B, MTAP16, MTAP24) that bundle several NAL units, which helps when a wired network allows roughly 1500 bytes but a wireless system prefers 254 bytes or less. Types 28 and 29 are fragmentation units (FU-A, FU-B) that split one NAL unit over several packets.

A STAP groups NAL units that share the same time. Each is preceded by a 16-bit size. An MTAP groups NAL units with different times, adding an 8-bit decoding order number difference and a 16-bit or 24-bit timestamp offset to each unit. The packet's RTP timestamp is set to the earliest time of the units inside. Aggregation packets MUST NOT be nested and MUST NOT contain fragmentation units.

Fragmentation lets a NAL unit larger than 64 kbytes cross an IPv4 network and lets forward error correction be applied to a single NAL unit. Fragments go out in consecutive RTP sequence numbers. The FU header carries a Start bit, an End bit, a reserved bit and the original 5-bit type, and Start and End MUST NOT both be set in one FU. If a fragment is lost, the receiver SHOULD discard the following fragments of that NAL unit.
sections.eli5: Little pieces can share one envelope, and a huge piece can be cut up and sent in several envelopes. Each envelope's label says which of the two it is.

sections.title: Packetization Modes and Decoding Order
sections.content:
Three modes control which packet types are allowed, and they are selected by the OPTIONAL packetization-mode parameter. Single NAL unit mode (value 0 or absent) MUST be supported by all receivers and suits systems compatible with ITU-T H.241. Non-interleaved mode (value 1) SHOULD be supported and also allows STAP-A and FU-A. Interleaved mode (value 2) may be supported by some receivers and allows STAP-B, MTAPs, FU-A and FU-B, so NAL units can be sent out of decoding order.

To restore order, the interleaved packet types carry a decoding order number (DON) from 0 to 65535 that wraps around. STAP-B and FU-B carry a DON directly, and MTAPs give a DON base plus a per-unit difference. When the sprop-interleaving-depth parameter is 0 or absent, transmission order MUST match decoding order. The RFC also defines the function don_diff(m,n) for comparing DON values across the wrap.

MANEs MUST NOT duplicate any NAL unit, except that sequence or picture parameter set NAL units MAY be duplicated to make their reception more probable.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to pack and send. The simple way sends one piece per envelope in order. The cleverer way mixes the order on purpose, so every piece gets a number to let the receiver sort them again.

sections.title: De-Packetization
sections.content:
The RFC describes de-packetization as an example, since the process is implementation dependent. Any scheme is fine if it produces the same NAL units in the same order. In single NAL unit and non-interleaved modes the receiver works in RTP sequence number order: single NAL units go straight to the decoder, STAP-A contents go in packet order, and FU-A fragments are concatenated.

In interleaved mode the receiver uses a de-interleaving buffer. Initial buffering ends when the buffer holds N or more VCL NAL units (N being sprop-interleaving-depth plus 1), when the DON spread exceeds sprop-max-don-diff, or when sprop-init-buf-time has elapsed. NAL units then leave the buffer in ascending DON distance order. Receivers are recommended to size the buffer at least as large as sprop-deint-buf-req.

Intelligent receivers or gateways that must drop packets should first drop those with NRI equal to 0. Dropping any packet with a larger NRI very likely leads to decoder drift and SHOULD be avoided.
sections.eli5: The receiver keeps incoming pieces in a waiting tray until enough have arrived. Then it hands them over in numbered order. If it has to throw some away, it starts with the least important ones.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters and SDP
sections.content:
The media type is video/H264 with no required parameters. Optional parameters select features and describe the stream. Those starting with sprop describe stream properties. profile-level-id is a hexadecimal form of three bytes from the sequence parameter set (profile_idc, profile-iop and level_idc) and gives the default sub-profile and level. If it is absent, the Baseline profile without additional constraints at Level 1 MUST be inferred. max-recv-level and a family of max-* parameters let a receiver signal capabilities beyond the default level.

The RFC maps the parameters into SDP and describes use with the SDP Offer/Answer model (RFC 3264) and in declarative session descriptions. It also gives guidance on parameter sets: send them out of band before the session or in-band, put them in-band with reliable delivery such as repetition, FEC or retransmission, and do not use both out-of-band updates and in-band updates in the same session unless synchronised. Two informative procedures show how an encoder can answer a request for a decoder refresh point, by sending an IDR picture or by gradual recovery.
sections.eli5: Before the call starts, both sides swap a short form listing what video they can handle, like agreeing on which language and speed to use.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Streams are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3550. Confidentiality comes from encryption such as SRTP (RFC 3711), and since the compression is end to end, encryption has to be applied after it. The RFC warns of a denial-of-service threat: an attacker can inject pathological packets that are costly to decode, and H.264 is particularly vulnerable because NAL units can affect the decoding of many later ones. Data origin authentication and integrity protection of at least the RTP packet is RECOMMENDED. Decoders MUST be cautious with user data SEI messages.

End-to-end protection stops a MANE from doing anything beyond discarding whole packets, and confidentiality even prevents that, so a MANE must be a trusted entity in the security context. For congestion control, RFC 3550 and the applicable profile apply, and best-effort users MUST monitor packet loss, which is acceptable if a TCP flow in the same conditions would get no more throughput.
sections.eli5: Video can be locked so nobody can peek. Someone could still send tricky pieces that overload the viewer, so the sender should be checked. Also, a video stream has to slow down if the network gets crowded.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3984
sections.content:
This memo obsoletes RFC 3984. The technical changes include bug fixes and new media type parameters (max-smbps, sprop-level-parameter-sets, use-level-src-parameter-sets, in-band-parameter-sets, sar-understood and sar-supported), plus max-recv-level and level-asymmetry-allowed. The parameter-add parameter was removed. The rules for the SDP Offer/Answer model were revised, including that the level can be downgraded in an answer.

Most legacy implementations still interwork. Problems can arise only when parameter sets are sent out of band. Declarative uses such as RTSP and SAP may need two sets of streams, because a legacy receiver cannot accept SDP with an unrecognised parameter.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. It adds new options and fixes some mistakes. Mostly the old and new versions still work together.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Forbidden zero bit; 1 means possible bit errors or syntax violations.

fields.name: NRI
fields.desc: Importance of the NAL unit; 00 means it can be discarded safely.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: NAL unit type, which also selects the payload structure.
